parole.significato: Added to a stem to form a patronymic or matronymic surname.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German -berg.

parole.significato: Forms nouns for a discrete living organism that has a specified mode of living.
parole.testo: Probably from German, modification of Ancient Greek βῐούντ- (bĭoúnt-), βιῶν (biôn, “living”), present participle of βῐοῦν (bĭoûn, “to live”), from βῐ́ος (bĭ́os, “mode of life”).

parole.significato: A synthetic alkaloid used as a local anesthetic.
parole.testo: From German -kain, extracted from the word Kokain (“cocaine”), because cocaine was formerly used as a local anaesthetic.

parole.significato: A festival, a fest; used in names of events.
parole.testo: From fest, from German Fest (“festival”).

parole.significato: An expert on the specified subject.
parole.testo: From meister, from German Meister (“master”, “champion”).

parole.significato: a ketone
parole.testo: Clipping of ketone, which was analogous to margarone. Further etymology is unclear.

parole.significato: Added to a stem to form a patronymic or matronymic surname.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German -stein.

parole.significato: Added to a stem to form a patronymic or matronymic surname.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German -witz.

parole.significato: A homosexual in Germany in the era when homosexuality was illegal (1871 to 1994).
parole.testo: Borrowed from German 175er.

parole.significato: A rare heavy tank that the German Reich deployed in 1918.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German A7V.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the city of Aachen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Aachener, equal to Aachen + -er.

parole.significato: The occurrence of proteolytic enzymes specific for foreign proteins introduced via parents.
parole.testo: Calque of German Abderhaldensche Reaktion, named after Swiss chemist Emil Abderhalden.

parole.significato: The theory that humanity's morality will never advance beyond its present state.
parole.testo: From German Abderitismus, from Abderit (“foolish person”) + -ismus (“-ism”), from Ancient Greek Ἀβδηρῑ́της (Abdērī́tēs, “Abderite”) because of the Abderites’ famed foolishness and stupidity in classical Greece. It is equivalent to Abderite + -ism. The German term was coined by the philosopher Immanu

parole.significato: An evening performance of religious music.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Abendmusik (literally “evening music”); Abend (“evening”) + Musik (“music”).

parole.significato: Repetition of the same word or phrases for emphasis; epistrophe, especially the concluding section.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Abgesang; ab- (“down, from”) + Gesang (“song”).

parole.significato: Outrageous; tasteless.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German abgeschmackt.

parole.significato: A group of matriculation exams taken in the final year of German secondary school.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Abitur.

parole.significato: A pupil / student in the German education system who is taking, or who has taken and passed, the Abitur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Abiturient, from Latin abituriō (“to wish to leave”).

parole.significato: The substitution of one root vowel for another, thus indicating a corresponding modification of use or meaning; vowel p…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ablaut (“sound gradation”), which is from ab- or ab (“down, off”), + Laut (“sound”). Ab is used here in the sense of “deviating, varying” as in Abgott (“god other than the true God”), Abart (“different sort, variety, anomality”).

parole.significato: A red ocher used to darken mahogany and for making chloride of potassium.
parole.testo: From German abräumen (“to remove”), from ab (“from”) (Old High German aba (“away”)) + raum (“space”) (Old High German rūm).

parole.significato: To eliminate previously repressed emotions by reliving past experiences.
parole.testo: Partial calque of German abreagieren, from ab (“away from, off, down from”) + reagieren (“to react”), equivalent to ab- + react.

parole.significato: The re-living of an experience with a view to purging its emotional dross.
parole.testo: Partial calque of German Abreagierung, from ab (“away from”) + Reagierung (“reaction”).

parole.significato: Antilock brake.
parole.testo: Calque of German Antiblockiersystem.

parole.significato: To descend a steep or vertical drop using a rope with a mechanical friction device or (classic abseil) by wrapping the…
parole.testo: From German abseilen, from ab- (“down”) + Seil (“rope”).

parole.significato: Of a language or dialect (a lect), being different from another lect in its intrinsic linguistic features (as opposed t…
parole.testo: From German Abstandsprache.

parole.significato: The right to teach, learn, and (communicate) research freely without unreasonable interference from authority, or fear…
parole.testo: Calque of German akademische Freiheit. First attested in English in 1901.

parole.significato: A box-shaped musical instrument played by compressing or expanding its bellows while pressing its buttons or its keys,…
parole.testo: First attested in 1831. Borrowed from German Akkordeon, from Akkord (“harmony”), from French accord, from Old French acorder, based on Italian accordare (“to tune”). See also accord.

parole.significato: The guttural phoneme /x/ (the voiceless velar fricative) of the German language, the sound of the letters ch in German…
parole.testo: From German Ach-Laut, ach-Laut, from ach (which has this sound) + Laut (“sound”).

parole.significato: Total color blindness; the total inability to distinguish colors due to the absence of cone cells in the eyes.
parole.testo: From German Achromatopsie, from Ancient Greek ἀχρώματος (akhrṓmatos), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”), + -opsie. By surface analysis, a- + chromato- + -opsia.

parole.significato: Synonym of octad.
parole.testo: Equivalent to German acht (“eight”) + Beine (“legs”).

parole.significato: meticulous, painstaking, thorough
parole.testo: From German akribisch (“meticulous”) or its etymon Ancient Greek ἀκριβής (akribḗs, “exact, accurate, precise”).

parole.significato: A pungent, acrid, poisonous liquid aldehyde, CH₂=CH-CH=O, made by the destructive distillation of glycerol.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Acrolein, from Latin acer (“sharp”) + oleō (“smell”, verb) + -in.

parole.significato: An abbreviation formed by the initial letters of other words.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Akronym (from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “end; peak”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”)), modelled after Homonym and Synonym, first attested in German in the early 1900s and in English in 1940. By surface analysis, acro- (prefix meaning ‘beginning; high’) + -onym (suffix meaning ‘name’)

parole.significato: A device that records the movements of a sleeping person.
parole.testo: From German Aktograph.

parole.significato: A base, C₅H₅N₅, found in certain glands and tissues, which pairs with thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA.
parole.testo: From German Adenin, from Ancient Greek ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”). By surface analysis, aden- + -ine. It was named in 1885 by the German biochemist Albrecht Kossel, in reference to the pancreas (a specific gland) from which Kossel's sample had been extracted.

parole.significato: A nucleoside derived from adenine and ribose, found in striated muscle tissue.
parole.testo: From German Adenosin, corresponding to aden(ine) + (rib)os(e) + -ine.

parole.significato: A clothing product made by Adidas, especially a pair of shoes.
parole.testo: From the German company name Adidas, after its founder, Adolf “Adi” Dassler.

parole.significato: chicken feet, skewered and grilled, sold as street food
parole.testo: Genericized trademark from the German company name, Adidas. The sense is most likely due to the association made with chicken feet and Adidas shoes. Compare Cebuano adidas and Tagalog adidas.

parole.significato: The adhesion of a liquid or gas on the surface of a solid material, forming a thin film on the surface.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Adsorption, from ad- + (Ab)sorption.

parole.significato: A calendar used to count down the days of Advent, having windows revealing a hidden picture or gift on each day.
parole.testo: Probably a calque of German Adventskalender, the modern tradition having originated in 19th-century Germany.

parole.significato: A string stop on an organ with a very soft tone.
parole.testo: From German Aeoline, from Classical Latin Aeolus (see Aeolian harp) + German -ine. Piecewise doublet of aeolina.

parole.significato: The growth of an organism either towards, or away from a region of higher oxygen content.
parole.testo: Formed as aero- + -tropism after the German Aërotropismus.

parole.significato: A breed of toy dog bred in Western Europe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Affenpinscher.

parole.significato: A major sulcus defining the primary visual cortex in apes and other monkey species.
parole.testo: From German Affenspalte.

parole.significato: A posterior subdivision of the hindbrain; the myelencephalon.
parole.testo: From after- + brain, a calque of German Nachhirn.

parole.significato: A medieval fief, which a liege lord received then subsequently enfeoffed wholly or partially to a vassal or vassals.
parole.testo: From German Afterlehen, from after- (“after, later”) + Lehen (“fief”).

parole.significato: a cell that divides by schizogony
parole.testo: From German Agamont, analyzable as Ancient Greek ἄγαμος (ágamos, “unmarried”) + -ont.

parole.significato: Accentuating a note by extending it slightly beyond its normal time value.
parole.testo: Apparently from German Agoge (“tempo”), from Ancient Greek ἀγωγή (agōgḗ, “carrying, leading, reduplicated formation; tempo”), + -ic, after German agogisch. By surface analysis, agoge + -ic.

parole.significato: A polearm used in Germany in the 15th century.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ahlspieß.

parole.significato: The spirit of one's future self, present in the moment, that quietly knows the plans others hold for you will not come…
parole.testo: German compound. From German ahnen (“to sense, to have a premonition; to intuit something not yet spoken”) (compare Ahnung (“foreboding, vague foreknowledge”) and Ahnen (“forebears, ancestors”)) and Geist (“spirit, ghost, mind”). The compound evokes a ghost that arrives from the future rather than t

parole.significato: A genealogical numbering system for listing a person's direct ancestors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ahnentafel (literally “ancestors table”).

parole.significato: a widespread body of air, the properties of which can be identified as: (a) having been established while that air was…
parole.testo: From air + mass. Perhaps a calque of German Luftmasse.

parole.significato: The route and aircraft used to deliver material by an airlift.
parole.testo: From air + bridge. In some cases, Calque of German Luftbrücke.

parole.significato: A retroflexion of the face at the front of the palate in primates.
parole.testo: Coined by Austrian zoologist Helmut Otto Hofer in 1952 as German Airorhynchie, from Ancient Greek ἀείρω (aeírō, “to raise, lift”) + ῥῠ́γχος (rhŭ́nkhos, “snout”).

parole.significato: larger pulk (low-slung boatlike sled, used for man-hauling supplies across snow and ice)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Akja, Swedish ackja, Finnish akkia, from older Finnish ahkio or older Sami akio, akje, ultimately from a Proto-Uralic *aškɜ, or Proto-Norse *ᚨᚲᛃᛟ (*akjō), corresponding to Swedish äcka, Icelandic ekja (“driving, fording”), to the root ak (Swedish åk), “drive, ford, ride”. Cognat

parole.significato: A property of verbs and other predicates indicating internal temporal nature; lexical aspect.
parole.testo: From German Aktionsart, from Aktion (“action”) + Art (“kind, sort”). Attested in English from the 19th century.

parole.significato: A type of development of certain diphthongs, especially in Anglo-Frisian, that was traditionally explained as the shift…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Akzentumsprung, from Akzent (“accent”) + Umsprung (“leap, sudden shift”).

parole.significato: abnormal bluish pigmentation in fish, caused by lack of guanine
parole.testo: From German Alampie, coined (as Alampia) by Karl Theodor Ernst von Siebold (1863), from Ancient Greek α- (a-, “not”) + λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”).

parole.significato: Inulin.
parole.testo: From German Alant (“elecampane”), + -in.

parole.significato: A short instrumental composition, usually performed on the piano and light in character.
parole.testo: From German Albumblatt (“album leaf”).

parole.significato: Any of a large class of reactive organic compounds (R·CHO) having a carbonyl functional group attached to one hydrocarb…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Aldehyd, a contraction of the Latin al(cohol) dehyd(rogenātum).

parole.significato: A mineralocorticoid hormone, secreted by the adrenal cortex, that regulates the balance of sodium and potassium in the…
parole.testo: From aldo- (“related to aldehydes”) + -sterone, modelled on German Aldosteron; coined in the 1950s.

parole.significato: A protective substance that exists in the serum or other bodily fluid and is capable of killing microorganisms; complem…
parole.testo: Ultimately from German Alexine, coined by Hans Buchner in 1891 from the Ancient Greek ἀλέξω (aléxō).

parole.significato: A physical condition that causes a person to gain sexual pleasure by suffering pain, particularly to erogenous zones.
parole.testo: From German Algolagnie, from Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) + λαγνεία (lagneía, “lust”). Equivalent to algo- + -lagnia.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being alimentive.
parole.testo: 1828, George Combe, from a German [Term?] term coined by Johann Spurzheim.

parole.significato: Any acyclic saturated hydrocarbon (methane, ethane, etc.).
parole.testo: From German Alkan, formed as alkyl + -ane.

parole.significato: homogentisic acid
parole.testo: From German Alkapton, coined by Boedeker (1861) as "an admittedly somewhat barbaric combination" of Alkali (“alkali”) + Ancient Greek κάπτον (kápton), neuter present participle of Ancient Greek κάπτω (káptō, “to gulp down”), after the tendency of alkapton to strongly react with oxygen in alkaline so

parole.significato: One of a number of alternative forms of the same gene occupying a given position, or locus, on a chromosome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Allel, shortened from Allelomorph, from English allelomorph. Ultimately from the Ancient Greek ἀλλήλων (allḗlōn, “each other”) from ἄλλος (állos, “other”).

parole.significato: A disorder of the immune system causing adverse reactions to substances (allergens) not harmful to most and marked by t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Allergie. Coined by Austrian pediatrician Clemens von Pirquet in 1906 from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”), on the model of Energie.

parole.significato: “Everything else is the work of man.” “Everything else is a human construct.”
parole.testo: A corruption of German mathematician Leopold Kronecker's finite dictum “die ganzen Zahlen hat Gott gemacht; alles andere ist Menschenwerk” : “God made the integers; everything else is the work of man”. The reason for the addition of an "s" to "andere" ("anderes" is grammatically incorrect and not pr

parole.significato: A system of heroic medicine that treats symptoms with substances that produce the opposite effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Allopathie, allo- + -pathy, originally a pejorative term.

parole.significato: A rosy or reddish glow seen during sunset or sunrise on the summits of mountains, especially snow-covered mountains on…
parole.testo: A partial calque of German Alpenglühen (literally “glow of the Alps”), with the second element replaced by the English equivalent glow.

parole.significato: A stout adjustable walking stick with a metal point, used by mountain climbers and walkers in hilly or uneven terrain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Alpenstock, from Alpen (“alps”) + Stock (“stick”), early 19th c.

parole.significato: A mountain-climber, especially one that uses an alpenstock.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German alpenstöcker.

parole.significato: An aragonite mineral consisting of an isomorphous mixture of calcium and barium carbonates.
parole.testo: After German Alstonit, from Alston Moor where it was discovered.

parole.significato: Synonym of altbier.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Alt.

parole.significato: A form of German top-fermenting beer that originated in Westphalia and later spread to parts of the Rhineland.
parole.testo: From German Altbier (literally “old beer”).

parole.significato: By definition or inherently; a priori.
parole.testo: Calque of German immer schon.

parole.significato: A disorder involving loss of mental functions resulting from brain tissue changes; senile dementia of the Alzheimer's t…
parole.testo: Named after Alois Alzheimer (1864–1915), a German neurologist who described the disease in 1906.

parole.significato: Any of several cherries cultivated from the sour cherry, distinguished from morellos by colorless juice.
parole.testo: From German Amarelle, from Medieval Latin amārellum, from Latin amārus (“bitter, sour”) + -ellum (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: An Inuit parka designed to carry a small child.
parole.testo: From German Amaut, from Danish amaut, ultimately from Greenlandic amaat.

parole.significato: Contradictory behaviors exhibited when one is pulled between different choices.
parole.testo: From ambi- + tendency, after German Ambitendenz.

parole.significato: The coexistence of opposing attitudes or feelings (such as love and hate) towards a person, object or idea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ambivalenz (“simultaneous conflicting feelings”), from Latin ambi- (“both”) and valentia (“strength”), from the verb valere (“to be strong”) (see valiant); spelled on the model of French-origin words ending in -ence. The German term was coined by Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler

parole.significato: Simultaneously experiencing or expressing opposing or contradictory feelings, beliefs, motivations, or meanings.
parole.testo: Back-formation from ambivalence, from German Ambivalenz, from Latin ambi- (“in two ways”) + valeō (“be strong”); equivalent to ambi- + -valent. Compare ambivert.

parole.significato: Any organic compound containing both an amino and a carboxylic acid functional group.
parole.testo: See amine and acid. Likely a calque of German Aminosäure, which is attested earlier.

parole.significato: An official in German-speaking countries of Europe in the Middle Ages, similar to a bailiff.
parole.testo: From German Amtmann.

parole.significato: A cultivar of the green or red pepper, Capsicum annuum, having long, tapering fruit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Anaheim (literally “home of Ana”). Likely a reference to the local Santa Ana River.

parole.significato: related to the Ancient North Arabian script or language(s)
parole.testo: Attested since 1904. Calque of German Alt-Nord-Arabisch (itself from 1870s), which corresponds to Altnordarabisch in modern orthography

parole.significato: The methods or techniques used to teach adults; adult education.
parole.testo: From andr- + -agogy, after German Andragogik.

parole.significato: fishing rod
parole.testo: Possibly a calque of German Angelrute or calque of Dutch hengelroede; equivalent to angle (“to fish”) + rod.

parole.significato: Synonym of Anglicist.
parole.testo: From German Anglist.

parole.significato: Synonym of English studies.
parole.testo: Modification of German Anglistik, from Anglist (“Anglist or Anglicist”) + -ik (“-ics”). By surface analysis, Anglo- + -ist + -ics, Anglo- + -istics, or Anglist + -ics.

parole.significato: Emotional turmoil; painful sadness; anguish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Angst or Danish angst; attested since the 19th century in English translations of the works of Søren Kierkegaard. Initially capitalized (as in German and contemporaneous Danish), the term first began to be written with a lowercase "a" around 1940–44. The German and Danish terms

parole.significato: The simplest aromatic amine, C₆H₅NH₂, synthesized by the reduction of nitrobenzene; it is a colourless oily basic poiso…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Anilin, coined by German chemist Carl Julius Fritzsche. From Portuguese anil (“indigo”) + -in (“-ine (organic compounds)”).

parole.significato: A primordium, the initial clustering of embryonic cells from which a body part develops.
parole.testo: From German Anlage.

parole.significato: The first sound of a word (word-initial position) or syllable (syllable-initial position).
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Anlaut, from an- (“on, at the beginning”) + Laut (“sound”).

parole.significato: A political system which is neither fully democratic nor fully autocratic, often being vulnerable to political instabil…
parole.testo: Apparently from an- + -ocracy, representing German Akratie.

parole.significato: An instrument used to test for color blindness by measuring quantitative and qualitative anomalies in color perception.
parole.testo: From German Anomaloskop, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “irregular, uneven”) (from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓- (ă-, “a-, prefix meaning ‘not’”) + ὁμᾰλός (homălós, “even, level”)) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look, to look at; to examine, to inspect”) (from Proto-Indo-European *sḱop, ultimately from *speḱ- (“

parole.significato: Any industrial structure whose architecture is thought to have unintended artistic qualities.
parole.testo: Calque of German Anonyme Skulpturen; the term was used by Bernd and Hilla Becher, who photographed such structures.

parole.significato: A mathematical assumption used to describe a certain phenomenon, posited in order to help provisionally solve an equati…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from German Ansatz.

parole.significato: Sense-perception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Anschauung, from anschauen (“to look at”).

parole.significato: Political annexation, specifically that of Austria into Nazi Germany in 1938.
parole.testo: From German Anschluss (“annexation”) (formerly Anschluß), from anschließen (“to join, unite”).

parole.significato: Someone with anti-Semitic views.
parole.testo: 1881, from German Antisemit (coined by Wilhelm Marr in 1879 as a scientific-sounding self-identification), from German antisemitisch (coined by Moritz Steinschneider in 1860), from anti- + semitisch

parole.significato: Relating to or exhibiting anti-Semitism.
parole.testo: From anti- + Semitic; calque of German antisemitisch, which was first used in 1860 by Jewish scholar Moritz Steinschneider. For more see anti-Semitism.

parole.significato: Prejudice, discrimination, hostility or political or religious opposition directed against ethnic or religious Jews or…
parole.testo: From German Antisemitismus. It is typically said that German political agitator Wilhelm Marr invented the term to replace Judenhaß (literally “Jew-hatred”) to make hatred of the Jews seem rational and sanctioned by scientific knowledge; Marr founded the Antisemitenliga ("Anti-Semites' League") in 18

parole.significato: A protein produced by B-lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
parole.testo: From anti- + body, a calque of German Antikörper.

parole.significato: A situation where one attempts to predict expectations others (particularly superiors) have, without explicit communica…
parole.testo: Semantic calque of German vorauseilender Gehorsam (literally “running ahead/in front of obediently”). Constructed from anticipatory + obedience.

parole.significato: A local instance of this movement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Antifa, originally an abbreviation for Antifaschistische Aktion, a wing of the Communist Party of Germany founded in 1932. Also a clipping of antifascism or antifascist.

parole.significato: One who declares himself king in opposition to a reigning monarch, especially in an electoral monarchy.
parole.testo: From anti- + king. Calque of German Gegenkönig.

parole.significato: Directly counteracting a symptom or pathological process.
parole.testo: Perhaps independently from anti- + -pathic, after German antipatisch.

parole.significato: An antiquarian bookshop.
parole.testo: From German Antiquariat.

parole.significato: A calcium fluoride phosphate of variable composition, sometimes used in the manufacture of fertilizer, as a gemstone, a…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from German Apatit (“apatite”). Apatit was coined by the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner (1749–1817), as follows: Ancient Greek ᾰ̓πᾰ́τη (ăpắtē, “deceit, fraud”) (as it is often mistaken for other minerals) + German -it (suffix forming nouns denoting

parole.significato: Synonym of Affenspalte.
parole.testo: Calque of German Affenspalte

parole.significato: apple strudel
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Apfelstrudel.

parole.significato: Clear, harmonious, and restrained.
parole.testo: Coined by German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche. From German apollinisch (“Apollonian”).

parole.significato: Plant reproduction without fertilization.
parole.testo: From German Apomixis, from apo- + mixis.

parole.significato: The perception of or belief in connectedness among unrelated phenomena.
parole.testo: From German Apophänie, from Ancient Greek ἀποφαίνω (apophaínō, “to appear”), from ἀπο- (apo-) and φαίνω (phaínō, “appear”), coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958.

parole.significato: A European, especially German, pharmacy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Apotheke. Doublet of bodega and boutique.

parole.significato: An apparatus; an instrument; a device.
parole.testo: From German Apparat and Russian аппара́т (apparát). Doublet of apparatus.

parole.significato: The inherent properties of a device which affect the way it is used by individuals across cultures.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Germanism, derived from Apparat (“apparatus, device, machine”) + Geist (“spirit”). Perhaps influenced by zeitgeist. Coined by American communications academic James E. Katz.

parole.significato: An Austrian pastry of apples, sugar, raisins, spice, etc in thin strudel dough or filo pastry.
parole.testo: Partial calque of German Apfelstrudel, equivalent to apple + strudel.

parole.significato: The intentional feature by which something indirectly given to consciousness is experienced as co-present or implied al…
parole.testo: From German Appräsentation, coined by Edmund Husserl from appräsentieren, from Latin ad- + praesentatio.

parole.significato: A being created and sustained by the power of the imagination and the concentration of thought.
parole.testo: From German, coined by Swiss philosopher Paracelsus (1493–1541).

parole.significato: A craftsman who has knowledge of a manufacturing secret (specifically in the area of porcelain manufacturing).
parole.testo: From arcane + -ist; in the sense of a craftsman with secret knowledge about porcelain manufacturing, borrowed from German Arcanist.

parole.significato: A head or chief butler
parole.testo: From arch- + butler, probably a calque of German Erzschenke.

parole.significato: The grand marshal of the Holy Roman Empire.
parole.testo: Calque of German Erzmarschall, equivalent to arch- + marshal.

parole.significato: A state of Germany that is not a city-state.

parole.significato: Poisoning caused by the toxin from Clostridium botulinum, an anaerobic bacterium that grows in improperly prepared food.
parole.testo: From German Botulismus, from Latin botulus (“sausage”), the first identified source of the disease, + -ism.

parole.significato: Either of the two highest trumps in the card games euchre and five hundred (where the joker is omitted).
parole.testo: From German Bauer. A doublet of etymology 2 and of the German-origin surname Bauer.

parole.significato: A breed of stocky, medium-sized, short-haired dog with a square-jawed muzzle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Boxer, from boxen (“to box (strike with the fists)”) + -er.

parole.significato: A kind of decoration for the breast of a coat, sometimes only a frog with a loop, but in some military uniforms enlarge…
parole.testo: * From German Brandenburg. * (city in Kentucky): Named after Solomon Brandenburg, a land owner.

parole.significato: Bratwurst.
parole.testo: Clipping of bratwurst, from German Bratwurst.

parole.significato: A large receptacle for cooking large-scale meals.
parole.testo: From German braten (“to pan-fry”).

parole.significato: A small (typically pork) sausage, usually served fried.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Bratwurst. The word is partly from braten (“to fry”) + Wurst (“sausage”), and partly from an older Middle High German brātwurst, in which brāt is an unrelated word meaning “ground meat” (compare German Brät). In modern German, the term Bratwurst is used almost exclusively for sa

parole.significato: An artist or writer who produces inferior work solely in order to earn a living.
parole.testo: Calque of German Brotkünstler (literally “bread artist”)

parole.significato: Broadtail.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Breitschwanz (literally “broad tail”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Bremen, Germany.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Bremer, equivalent to Brem(en) + -er.

parole.significato: The electromagnetic radiation produced by the deceleration of a charged particle, such as an electron, when it is defle…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Bremsstrahlung (“braking or deceleration radiation”), which had been coined in German by Arnold Sommerfeld from bremsen (“to brake”) + Strahlung (“radiation”) in 1909, and was first used in English by Arthur Edward Ruark and Harold Urey in 1930.

parole.significato: The moment in the path of a rocket when the fuel burns out, after which it continues its ballistic trajectory under onl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Brennschluss.

parole.significato: Members of any congregation in the Anabaptist tradition of the Schwarzenau Brethren, practicing credobaptism and commit…
parole.testo: Specific use of brethren as a semantic loan from German Brüder.

parole.significato: A person in charge of beer production at a brewery
parole.testo: From brew + master, a calque of German Braumeister.

parole.significato: A transparent scale that covers the eye of a snake and is periodically shed as part of the exuvia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Brille.

parole.significato: A prostitute, a woman of loose morals.
parole.testo: Early 20th century, apparent phono-semantic matching of German Braut (“bride”, also “girlfriend”, and more generally “broad, chick”).

parole.significato: A pungent colourless explosive liquid, CNO₂Br₃.
parole.testo: From German Brompikrin, from Brom (“bromine”) and the word for "picric (acid)".

parole.significato: A deep murmur.
parole.testo: From German Brüll (“a roar”).

parole.significato: A type of basket used to provide structure for breads during proofing.
parole.testo: From German Brotform, from Brot (“bread”) + Form (“shape”).

parole.significato: A uniformed member of the German Nazi Party (NSDAP), especially a storm trooper of the Sturmabteilung.
parole.testo: Calque of German Braunhemd, the nickname for a member of the Sturmabteilung, in reference to their brown uniforms. Equivalent to brown + shirt.

parole.significato: bun, bread roll
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Brötchen (“bread roll”).

parole.significato: The sum of the scores of all opponents in a competition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Buchholz

parole.significato: Sweet rolls made of enriched yeast dough, filled with powidl, jam, chocolate, ground poppy seeds or quark, brushed with…
parole.testo: From German Buchteln, plural of Buchtel.

parole.significato: Smoked herring.
parole.testo: From German Bückling or Swedish böckling. Cognate with Middle High German bockinc and Middle Dutch bocking (itself from bok (“buck”), referencing the foul smell).

parole.significato: A homeless person, usually a man.
parole.testo: 1864, back-formation from bummer, from German Bummler (“loafer”), from bummeln (“to loaf”).

parole.significato: A forager, especially in Sherman's March to the Sea of November to December 1864.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Bummler (“a drifter, a stroller, a rambler, a loiterer, a laggard”).

parole.significato: A league or confederacy; especially the confederation of German states.
parole.testo: From German Bund (“alliance, league”). Doublet of Bund, bond, and band.

parole.significato: A baking pan with a hollow, circular, raised area in the middle.
parole.testo: From German Bundkuchen, from Bund (“tied together”) + Kuchen (“cake”).

parole.significato: The military governor of a town or castle in the Middle Ages, especially in German-speaking Europe; a nobleman of the s…
parole.testo: From German Burggraf, from Burg (“castle”) + Graf (“count”). Compare Dutch burggraaf, French burgrave. See margrave.

parole.significato: A German university student.
parole.testo: From German Bursche.

parole.significato: A German open sandwich.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Butterbrot (literally “butter bread”).

parole.significato: Synonym of burgomaster.
parole.testo: From German Bürgermeister.

parole.significato: A kind of spicy smoked Australian sausage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Cabanossi, Kabanossi, from Polish kabanosy, nominative plural of kabanos.

parole.significato: The process by which two masses of water with different temperatures and salinities mix to form a new water mass with a…
parole.testo: From German Kabbelung; according to Foster (1972), the German word was first applied to the phenomenon by Witte (1902), and subsequently used in an anglicized form by Stommel (1960) and others.

parole.significato: Synonym of Wunderkammer.
parole.testo: Calque of German Wunderkammer (“room of wonders”); cabinet is intended in the (obsolete) sense "chamber, private room."

parole.significato: The theories and practices of the cameralists.
parole.testo: From German Kameralismus, from Medieval Latin cameralis + Latin -ismus (“-ism”). First element is from camera (“chamber”) (English camera), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára).

parole.significato: A public administrative servant of continental rulers of the 17th and 18th centuries who was a mercantilist and advocat…
parole.testo: From German Kameralist, from New Latin cameralista, from Medieval Latin cameralis + Latin -ista (“-ist”), from camera (“chamber”) (English camera), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára). Sense is due to administrators in the royal chamber; compare political sense of cabinet.

parole.significato: Military forces considered to be expendable.
parole.testo: Mid-19th century, from cannon (“artillery piece”) + fodder (“food”), a calque of German Kanonenfutter, itself possibly a calque of English food for powder. See the German for more.

parole.significato: To caress, fondle, or pet (someone); also, to have sexual intercourse with (someone); to make love with.
parole.testo: The origin of the verb is uncertain; the following possibilities have been suggested: * From a blend of ca(ress) + noodle (“to engage in frivolous behavior; to fool around or waste time; to mess around, to play”). * From German knuddeln (“to cuddle; (originally) to embrace tightly”); or related to L

parole.significato: The private orchestra or band of a prince or church.
parole.testo: From German Kapelle. Doublet of chapel.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to capitalism or to capitalists.
parole.testo: From capitalist + -ic, probably after German kapitalistisch. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-.

parole.significato: A chemical compound found in chilli peppers, which is responsible for their piquancy.
parole.testo: Arbitrary alteration of earlier capsicine, capsicin (“material extracted from cayenne pepper”), presumably to prevent confusion, from German Capsicin, from New Latin capsicum + German -in. Name introduced by John Clough Thresh (1850–1932) in “Capsaicin, the Active Principle of Capsicum Fruits”.

parole.significato: A volatile alkaloid extracted from Capsicum annuum or from capsaicin.
parole.testo: From German Capsicin, from New Latin Capsicum + German -in.

parole.significato: A metal link with a gate that can open and close, generally used for clipping ropes to anchors or other objects or for…
parole.testo: Shortened from German Karabinerhaken (“carbine hook”), reflecting that such a link was used for gear slinging even before it was used for rock climbing.

parole.significato: of, relating to or containing carbolic acid
parole.testo: Derived from German Carbolsäure (modern German Karbolsäure), which was coined in 1834 by its discoverer Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge. By surface analysis, carb- + -ol + -ic.

parole.significato: phenol (C₆H₅OH)
parole.testo: Partial calque of German Carbolsäure (modern German Karbolsäure), which was coined in 1834 by its discoverer Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge.

parole.significato: A betaine, 3-hydroxy-4-trimethylammonio-butanoate, that is found in the liver and has a function in fatty acid transpor…
parole.testo: From German Carnitin, coined from Latin carn- + Latin -i- + -t- (“arbitrary insertion”) + -in, for it was first described in meat extracts in 1905. By surface analysis, Latin carnit- + -ine.

parole.significato: A group of businesses or nations that collude to limit competition within an industry or market.
parole.testo: In the business sense, borrowed from German Kartell, first used by Eugen Richter in 1871 in the Reichstag. In the political sense, which was the vehicle for this metaphor, the English sense, like the German sense, was borrowed from French cartel in the sixteenth century, from Italian cartello, dimin

parole.significato: A type of early cannon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kartaune, from Italian quartana (“25-pounder cannon”).

parole.significato: A piece of instrumental music of the eighteenth century similar to the serenade, and often performed outdoors.
parole.testo: From German Kassation, from Italian cassazione

parole.significato: mica
parole.testo: Calque of German Katzensilber

parole.significato: An abrupt loss of muscle tone, sometimes associated with narcolepsy.
parole.testo: From German Kataplexie, from Ancient Greek κατάπληξις (katáplēxis), from κατά (katá, “down”) + πλῆξῐς (plêxĭs, “blow, act of striking”).

parole.significato: A fundamental ethical principle intended as a guide for determining whether any contemplated action is morally right, b…
parole.testo: From German kategorischer Imperativ.

parole.significato: To focus one's emotional energies on someone or something.
parole.testo: Back-formation from cathexis and cathectic. A loan creation coined by British psychoanalyst James Strachey translating Freud’s German besetzen.

parole.significato: Any of a family of proteases primarily active within lysosomes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kathepsin, from Ancient Greek καθέψω (kathépsō), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕψω (hépsō, “boil”).

parole.significato: battle of encirclement
parole.testo: Calque of German Kesselschlacht. Compare kettle (“to contain demonstrators in a confined area; group of protesters or rioters confined in a limited area”).

parole.significato: A hypothetical subconscious agency which filters unacceptable thought before it reaches the conscious mind.
parole.testo: From an incorrect translation of German Zensur (“censorship”).

parole.significato: The overseer of a hundred (zent) in medieval France and Germany.
parole.testo: From German Zentgraf, from Latin cent- (“100”) + German -graf (“-grave”).

parole.significato: One of two major dialect groups of the High German language which is spoken primarily in central Germany, Luxembourg, e…
parole.testo: Calque of German Mitteldeutsch/mitteldeutsch.

parole.significato: The central region of a eukaryotic chromosome where the kinetochore is assembled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Centromer, corresponding to centro- + -mere (from Ancient Greek μέρος (méros, “part”)).

parole.significato: One who smokes continuously, by lighting one cigarette when they finish another, as in a chain.
parole.testo: From chain + smoker, calque of German Kettenraucher.

parole.significato: A battle between a deity and primordial chaos, especially in ancient Near Eastern mythology and/or religion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Chaoskampf (literally “chaos struggle”).

parole.significato: A musical composition that expresses a specific mood or non-musical idea.
parole.testo: Calque of German Charakterstück.

parole.significato: A regional currency used in Prien am Chiemsee, Bavaria, Germany, pegged to the euro and intended to promote local comme…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Chiemgauer, named after the Chiemgau region.

parole.significato: The musical director of a choir, who conducts performances and supervises rehearsal.
parole.testo: From choir + master, a calque of German Chormeister. Piecewise doublet of chorusmaster.

parole.significato: Stimulating the production of bile by the liver.
parole.testo: From German cholereticum, from modern Latin choleresis (“bile secretion from the liver”) (modelled on diuretic).

parole.significato: A form of Lutheran or Protestant hymn tune.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Choral.

parole.significato: A small Christmas gift for children symbolizing Jesus Christ as the “light” of the world. A typical modern Christingle…
parole.testo: Uncertain; according to the Oxford English Dictionary, possibly from dialectal German Christkindl, Christkindle (“the Christ child, believed to deliver presents to children on Christmas Eve; the presents so brought”), from Christ (“Christ”) + Kindl, Kindle (dialectal diminutive of Kind (“child”)). T

parole.significato: A Christmas decoration in the shape of an infant Jesus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Christkindl.

parole.significato: A Christmas market (Kris Kringle Mart).
parole.testo: From German Christkindlmarkt.

parole.significato: An evergreen tree (usually a conifer), or an artificial tree made to resemble this, which is typically decorated with l…
parole.testo: PIE word  *dóru From Christmas + tree, a calque of German Weynacht Baum (obsolete, 17th c.), Weihnachtsbaum, from Weynacht, Weihnacht (literary or poetic variant of Weihnachten (“Christmas”)) + -s- (genitive interfix) + Baum (“tree”). parole.significato: A monogram that forms an abbreviation for the name of Jesus Christ, traditionally used as a Christian symbol, such as t…
parole.testo: From Christo- + gram, c. 1900, adopted from German Christogramm, in c. 1860 as portmanteau or abbreviation of the slightly older (1840s) and more formal compound Christusmonogramm, translating the Medieval Latin monogramma Christi. English literature before 1900 used compositional "Monogram of Chris

parole.significato: A complex of DNA, RNA and proteins within the cell nucleus out of which chromosomes condense during cell division.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Chromatin, from (combining form of) Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + -ινος (-inos, “made of”). Analyzable as chromatic (“of colour”) + -in (“substance”).

parole.significato: The visual output from a chromatograph, usually a graphical display or histogram.
parole.testo: From German Chromatogramm, which was coined by Mikhail Tsvet in 1906.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to chromatography.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German chromatographisch; see there for more.

parole.significato: Any of various techniques for the qualitative or quantitative separation of the components of mixtures of compounds; al…
parole.testo: Back-formation from chromatographic, borrowed from German chromatographisch (see there for more); by surface analysis, chromato- + -graphy. The technique is so named because it was developed primarily for the separation of the plant pigments, which would separate in bands of different "colors" (chro

parole.significato: A linear arrangement of condensed DNA and associated proteins (such as chaperone proteins) which contains the genetic m…
parole.testo: 19th century: from German Chromosom, ultimately from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”) (because they are stained under the microscope). Equivalent to chromo- + -some.

parole.significato: An automobile of this make. (Formerly, often used as an example of a luxury car (mid-20th century).)
parole.testo: From the motor company founded by and named after Walter Chrysler in 1925. Surname derives from German Kreißler.

parole.significato: Having fleshy / succulent stems
parole.testo: From German chylocaul (from chyl- + Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós, “stem”)) + English -ous.

parole.significato: A sovereign city, as in Ancient Greece, often part of a league of such cities.
parole.testo: From city + state, a calque of German Stadtstaat.

parole.significato: An individual's awareness of their relative place within the class system of society.
parole.testo: Calque of German Klassenbewusstsein.

parole.significato: The enemy of a class, in particular the working class.
parole.testo: Calque of German Klassenfeind.

parole.significato: A keyboard, especially of a musical instrument.
parole.testo: From German Klaviatur, ultimately from Latin clāvis (“key”).

parole.significato: An early keyboard instrument producing a soft sound by means of metal blades (called tangents) attached to the inner en…
parole.testo: From German Klavichord, from Renaissance Latin clavichordium, from clāvis (“key”) + chorda (“cord, string”).

parole.significato: An elite group of intellectuals; learned people, the literati.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κλῆρος (klêros) + -isy. Introduced by Coleridge, based on German Clerisei (modern Klerisei), from Late Latin clēricus.

parole.significato: The sound of a horse's shod hoof striking the ground.
parole.testo: Perhaps from German or Dutch kloppen (“to hit, knock”), from Middle Dutch cloppen (“to make a clopping sound”), of onomatopoeic origin. See also clap.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Co) with an atomic number of 27: a hard, lustrous, silver-gray metal.
parole.testo: From German Kobalt, formerly also Kobald, ‑olt, ‑old, ‑elt, ‑el, apparently the same word as Kobold (“goblin”), from Middle High German, which became also a Harz Mountains silver miners’ term for rock laced with arsenic and sulfur, so called because it degraded the ore and made the miners ill. Doubl

parole.significato: The phenomenon where an attempted solution to a problem has an unintended consequence that makes the original problem w…
parole.testo: From cobra + effect, a calque of German Kobra-Effekt, coined by the German economist Horst Siebert (1938–2009) in a 2001 book, from an anecdote about an incident during the British rule of colonial India in the 19th century in which the government, concerned about the large number of venomous cobras

parole.significato: A social gathering for conversation while drinking coffee.
parole.testo: Partial calque of German Kaffeeklatsch.

parole.significato: sexual intercourse interrupted by withdrawal of the penis before ejaculation
parole.testo: Borrowed from the German Coitus interruptus, a Latinism of Coitus (the then standard spelling of Koitus) and interruptus (Latin for “interrupted”) in 1886, a year after its German coining. parole.significato: A sparkling red wine, often made by blending champagne with red wine, sometimes with additional flavorings added.
parole.testo: Calque of German kalte Ente, from kalten Ende (“cold end”). Attested in English from the 1960s, see quotations below.

parole.significato: A feeling of nervousness or anxiety causing one to reconsider a decision about an upcoming event.
parole.testo: Idiomatic sense possibly from a calque of German kalte Füße bekommen (“to get cold feet”), or of Lombard avegh minga frecc i pee (“to have no money”, literally “to be cold in the feet”) (Italian aver freddo ai piedi), said by a person who wishes to stop gambling, allegedly because the person now has

parole.significato: A planned economy in which the government (or some other central authority) is solely responsible for resource allocati…
parole.testo: Calque of German Befehlswirtschaft (“command economy”).

parole.significato: Being able to decide whether a jurisdictional entity has the power to hear a case.
parole.testo: Calque of German Kompetenz-Kompetenz.

parole.significato: Uncompromising; uncompromisable.
parole.testo: From compromise + -less. Non-native use influenced by German kompromisslos or Norwegian Bokmål kompromissløs.

parole.significato: A psychiatric disorder characterised by recurrent compulsions or compulsive ideas; obsessive-compulsive disorder.
parole.testo: Translating German Zwangsneurose.

parole.significato: The first violin in a symphony orchestra, which normally plays violin solos.
parole.testo: From concert + master, as a calque of German Konzertmeister. Piecewise doublet of concertmeister.

parole.significato: Synonym of concertmaster.
parole.testo: A partial calque of German Konzertmeister; from concert + meister. Piecewise doublet of concertmaster.

parole.significato: A female concertmaster.
parole.testo: Possibly a calque of German Konzertmeisterin, corresponding to concert + mistress.

parole.significato: Synonym of phosphorus match, a strike-anywhere friction match.
parole.testo: From German Congreve, after William Congreve, British rocket pioneer and administrator of the Imperial Continental Gas Association during the 1820s.

parole.significato: Joined together in pairs.
parole.testo: Inflected form of conjugate. Adjective sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Konjugation, konjugieren, coined 1899 by German chemist Johannes Thiele.

parole.significato: councillor of the consistory
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Consistorialrath, obsolete spelling of Konsistorialrat.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an utterance relaying information and likely to be regarded as true or false.
parole.testo: Coined to translate the German konstatierend, using cōnstāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of the Latin verb cōnstō (“to agree, correspond, or fit; to am certain, decided, or consistent”), suffixed with the English -ive, suggesting a hypothetical Latin etymon of the form *cōnstātīvus.

parole.significato: Counterproductive.
parole.testo: From contra- + productive. Spontaneously calqued from the users' respective native language, e.g. German kontraproduktiv, Romanian contraproductiv.

parole.significato: A non-finite verb form that serves to express adverbial subordination.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Konverb. By surface analysis, con- + verb; compare adverb and conjunctive.

parole.significato: A book or an encyclopedia of recipes and cookery tips.
parole.testo: From cook + book; possibly also a calque of German Kochbuch, from kochen (“cook”) + Buch (“book”).

parole.significato: cupronickel
parole.testo: Calque of German Kupfernickel. Piecewise doublet of cupronickel and kupfernickel.

parole.significato: The study of the evolution of the forms of nationalities, ethnicities, races, etc. by observing the supposed ontogenic…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from German Cormogenie, itself from Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós) + -genie; equivalent to Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “tree-trunk”) + -geny (“origin”). By surface analysis, cormo- + -geny.

parole.significato: The direct study of the evolution of the forms of nationalities, ethnicities, races, etc. rather than observation of it…
parole.testo: Simplified learned borrowing from German Cormophylogenie, itself from Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós) + Phylogenie; equivalent to a reduction of Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós) + phylogeny to Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “tree-trunk”) + -phyly (“tribehood”). By surface analysis, cormo- + -phyly.

parole.significato: The transference of a therapist's own unconscious feelings to their patient; unconscious or instinctive emotion felt to…
parole.testo: From counter- + transference, a calque of German Gegenübertragung.

parole.significato: Curonian; of, from, or pertaining to Courland
parole.testo: From German kurisch.

parole.significato: Curonian; of, from, or pertaining to Courland
parole.testo: From German kurländisch.

parole.significato: To devastate by heavy bombing.
parole.testo: From Coventry + -ate (verb-forming suffix), following German coventrieren. Coventry, England, was devastated by German firebombing in November 1940, during World War II.

parole.significato: A drink of rum mixed with sugar and set alight before drinking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Crambambuli.

parole.significato: A pair of conjoined twins joined at the head.
parole.testo: From German Kraniopagus, equivalent to cranio- + -pagus.

parole.significato: The process of industrial mutation that continually revolutionizes the economic structure from within.
parole.testo: Calque of German schöpferische Zerstörung, popularized by economist Joseph Schumpeter.

parole.significato: One of a Native American tribe from the Southeastern United States, also known as the Muscogee.
parole.testo: * As an English surname, from Creake in Norfolk, a variant of the noun crag (“steep rugged cliff”). * Also as an English surname, from the archaic noun cratch (“crib, manger”). * As a German surname, Americanized from Krieg (“war, warfare”), Krück, Kruck (see Krug (“jug”) and Krücke (“crutch”)), Kri

parole.significato: A pale yellow oily liquid, containing phenols and similar compounds, obtained by the destructive distillation of wood t…
parole.testo: From German Kreosot in the 1830s, coined in 1832 by German natural philosopher Carl Ludwig, Baron Reichenbach, from Ancient Greek κρέας (kréas, “flesh”) + σωτήρ (sōtḗr, “preserver”) for its use as an antiseptic and meat-preservative. The creosote bush was named after its scent. By surface analysis,

parole.significato: The examination and critique of society and literature, drawing from knowledge across social science and the humanities…
parole.testo: Calque of German kritische Theorie, first defined by Max Horkheimer in his 1937 essay “Traditional and Critical Theory”.

parole.significato: The sacrum.
parole.testo: From cross + bone, a calque of German Kreuzbein (“sacrum”).

parole.significato: The wearing of clothing which society considers appropriate for the opposite sex rather than the wearer's sex.
parole.testo: From cross- + dressing, a calque of German Transvestismus.

parole.significato: A cowhide with the belly and neck removed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Croupon, from French croupon, from Middle French crepon, from Old French crepon, from crope (“buttocks”) + -on.

parole.significato: sauerkraut
parole.testo: Adaptation of German Kraut.

parole.significato: Empetrum; a small genus of dwarf evergreen shrubs that bear edible fruit.
parole.testo: From crow + berry; probably a calque of German Krähenbeere. Apparently so-called due to birds' fondness for the fruit. parole.significato: In Austria-Hungary, any of the provinces, or largest administrative divisions of the monarchy.
parole.testo: Calque of German Kronland.

parole.significato: Any of several related simple woodwind instruments having a bent horn
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Krum(m)horn (literally “bent horn”).

parole.significato: Someone accused of cultural Bolshevism.
parole.testo: Calque of German Kulturbolschewist.

parole.significato: A political struggle for control over cultural institutions.
parole.testo: Calque of German Kulturkampf.

parole.significato: An alloy of copper containing from 10 to 40% nickel.
parole.testo: From cupro- + nickel, likely a calque of German Kupfernickel. Piecewise doublet of copper-nickel and kupfernickel.

parole.significato: A German national dish consisting of hot pork sausage cut into slices and seasoned with curry ketchup.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Currywurst, from Curry + Wurst (“sausage”). By surface analysis, curry + wurst.

parole.significato: That part of a cell (especially the nucleus) in which its development takes place
parole.testo: From German Cytoblast, equivalent to cyto- + -blast.

parole.testo: Borrowed from German Zytoplasma, Cytoplasma. Equivalent to cyto- (“cell”) + -plasm (“contents of a cell”).

parole.significato: A certain breed of dog having short legs and a long trunk, including standard-sized, miniature (smooth-haired, long-hai…
parole.testo: From German Dachshund (literally “badger dog”), from German Dachs (“badger”) + Hund (“dog”).

parole.significato: An igneous, volcanic rock with a high iron content.
parole.testo: From German Dazit, from Latin Dācia (“greater Romania”). First used in 1863 by Austrian geologists Franz von Hauer and Guido Stache, in a description of the geology of Transylvania.

parole.significato: A motor car manufactured by this company
parole.testo: From German Daimler.

parole.significato: A suspended monorail, cable car or public transport system.
parole.testo: From Danglebahn, a compound of English dangle and German Bahn (“train”), by analogy with other rail transport systems such as U-bahn, Straßenbahn, etc.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Danzig (modern-day Gdańsk).
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Danziger, from Danzig.

parole.significato: The estimated number of unreported criminal cases.
parole.testo: Calque of German Dunkelziffer.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Darmstadt.
parole.testo: From German Darmstädter.

parole.significato: Being; especially the nature of being; existence, presence, hereness, suchness, essence
parole.testo: From German Dasein (“there-to be”), from da (“there”) + sein (“to be”).

parole.significato: Internet-oriented companies that have a large number of users and possess detailed personal information on them, presum…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Datenkraken, plural of Datenkrake, itself a compound of Daten (“data”) and Krake (“octopus”), invoking an imagery of such a company being an octopus having its virtual "tentacles" deeply penetrating its users' online habits.

parole.significato: A developmental stage of certain nematode larvae in which they exhibit increased durability.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dauer (“duration”).

parole.significato: The persistence of an abnormal characteristic – generally an environmentally induced trait – over several generations o…
parole.testo: From German Dauer + English modification.

parole.significato: A prolonged sleep therapy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dauerschlaf, from Dauer (“duration, length”) + Schlaf (“sleep”).

parole.significato: A language which genetically descends from an earlier parent language.
parole.testo: Probably a calque of German Tochtersprache.

parole.significato: An electric wooden experimental musical instrument, a kind of friction idiophone.
parole.testo: From German Dachs (“badger”) (since it can generate animal sounds) and saxophone.

parole.significato: The elements of the events of the preceding day that subsequently occur in a dream.
parole.testo: Calque of German Tagesreste, coined by Sigmund Freud.

parole.significato: The drive toward death and self-destruction.
parole.testo: Calque of German Todestrieb.

parole.significato: A desire, especially subconscious, for the death of oneself or of someone else.
parole.testo: From death + wish. Calque of German Todeswunsch.

parole.significato: Synonym of debrecener (A Hungarian sausage)
parole.testo: From German Debreciner; from Hungarian Debrecen.

parole.significato: Synonym of debrecener (A Hungarian sausage)

parole.significato: Synonym of debrecener (A Hungarian sausage)
parole.testo: From German Debreziner; from Hungarian Debrecen.

parole.significato: A frame or edge which limits the pulp and, consequently, the size of the resulting paper.
parole.testo: From German Deckel, diminutive of Decke (“covering”).

parole.significato: A psychological strategy used unconsciously by people to cope with harmful or stressful situations.
parole.testo: Calque of German Abwehrmechanismus, a concept in the Freudian model.

parole.significato: Sword.
parole.testo: From German Degen (“dagger”).

parole.significato: The lengthened grade that appears in words of a certain root group, or stem group, in the course of vocalic variations.
parole.testo: From German Dehnstufe, from dehnen (“to stretch”) + Stufe (“step”).

parole.significato: dehydrogenase
parole.testo: Formed as de- + hydr- + -ase, by analogy with the German Dehydrase.

parole.significato: A shop that sells cooked or prepared food ready for serving.
parole.testo: Attested since 1954. Clipping of delicatessen, from German Delikatessen, plural of Delikatesse (“delicacy, fine food”), from French délicatesse, derived from the adjective délicat, from Latin delicatus.

parole.significato: A shop that sells cooked or prepared foods ready for serving.
parole.testo: First attested 1864. From German Delikatessen, plural of Delikatesse (“delicacy, fine food”), at the time also spelled Delicatesse(n), from French délicatesse, from délicat (“fine”), from Latin delicatus (“alluring”). The sense of store is more recent, originating in ellipsis from the common attribu

parole.significato: A green garnet.
parole.testo: From German Demantoid, from archaic/obsolete Demant (“diamond”) + -oid, from Middle High German diemant, from Old French diamant.

parole.significato: schizophrenia
parole.testo: A Latin term coined by Arnold Pick in 1891, first used in German and later adopted into English. From the Latin dēmentia (“madness; insanity”) + praecox (“premature; untimely”, whence English precocious), together meaning “untimely madness” or “premature dementia”. parole.significato: Delusional parasitosis (delusional disorder in which individuals incorrectly believe they are infested with parasites,…
parole.testo: From German Dermatozoenwahn.

parole.significato: An organism that feeds on detritus.
parole.testo: From German Detritivore, from Latin dētrītus (“the act of rubbing away”) (from dēterō (“to rub away, to rub off, to wear out”), from dē- (“away; down”) + terō (“to rub; to wear away, to wear out”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, to rub by twisting; to twist, to turn”)) + Latin vorāre (fr

parole.significato: German, in the German language.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tewtéh₂ Borrowed from German Deutsch (“German”). Doublet of Dutch and Doitsu.

parole.significato: The former currency unit of Germany (now replaced by the euro), abbreviated as DM or DEM.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Deutsche Mark.

parole.significato: A German man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Deutscher.

parole.significato: A US marine.
parole.testo: Calque of German Teufelshund (“hound of Hell”, literally “Devil's hound”).

parole.significato: Foreign currency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Devisen.

parole.significato: The coming together of antagonistic groups around one issue on which they find common ground, for instance the rejectio…
parole.testo: From diagonal + -ism, based on German Querdenken (literally “diagonal thinking”). Coined by Canadian historian and professor Quinn Slobodian and political scientist William Callison in the context of the German Querdenker (“anti-vaxx”) movement during the COVID-19 pandemic, see quotations.

parole.significato: The concept of reality in which material things are in the constant process of change brought about by the tension betw…
parole.testo: Calque of German dialektischer Materialismus, coined by Joseph Dietzgen in Streifzüge eines Sozialisten in das Gebiet der Erkenntnißtheorie [1887].

parole.significato: That stimulates each ear with a different pitch or loudness
parole.testo: From German dichotisch, from Ancient Greek δῐ́χᾰ (dĭ́khă, “apart”) + οὖς (oûs), ὠτ- (ōt-, “ear”) + -isch (-ic).

parole.significato: Any of a family of glycoproteins that are involved in the development of the embryo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dickkopf (“stubborn person”, literally “thick head”), from the fact that Dickkopf-related protein 1 (DKK1), one of the dickkopf proteins, was found to be required for head formation in embryos. The word was coined by Andrei Glinka, Wei Wu, Hajo Delius, A. Paula Monaghan, Claudia

parole.significato: A socio-political power wherein the bourgeoisie collectively holds the most influence over politics and the masses, as…
parole.testo: Calque of German Diktatur der Bourgeoisie, which is attested earliest in Karl Marx's series The Class Struggles in France, 1848–1850 [1850].

parole.significato: A socio-political power characterized by a struggle to achieve a communist society, as opposed to the dictatorship of t…
parole.testo: Calque of German Diktatur des Proletariats. Initially worded as Diktatur der Arbeiterklasse “dictatorship of the working class” and Klassendiktatur des Proletariats “class dictatorship of the proletariat”, both attested earliest in Karl Marx's series The Class Struggles in France, 1848–1850 [1850].

parole.significato: A morgue worker responsible for handling, moving, and cleaning the corpse.
parole.testo: From German Diener (“servant”).

parole.significato: To ignite a substance by using the heat generated by compression.
parole.testo: From German Diesel, named after inventor Rudolf Diesel, who developed a heavy-duty engine in Germany (1892–1897) and perfected it throughout his life.

parole.significato: A dogmatic decree or command, especially issued by one who rules without popular consent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Diktat, from Latin dictātum (“that which has been dictated”), from the perfect passive participle of dictō (“dictate”). Doublet of dictate. Originally used with reference to Germany's penalties as dictated by the Treaty of Versailles.

parole.significato: Synonym of spelt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dinkel.

parole.significato: Wild, irrational, undisciplined, orgiastic.
parole.testo: From German dionysisch (“Dionysian”). Coined by German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche.

parole.significato: A traditional Alpine woman's dress having a tight bodice and full skirt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dirndl, a diminutive of Dirne (“girl”) (Austria, Bavaria), from Middle High German dierne (“girl; servant”), from Old High German diorna, thiorna (“girl; servant”), from Proto-West Germanic *þewernā (“maiden, young girl; female servant, handmaid”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Eur

parole.significato: The act of disenchanting or the state of being disenchanted.
parole.testo: From dis- + enchantment. In the social sciences sense a calque of German Entzauberung, as used by sociologist Max Weber.

parole.significato: Silly or scatterbrained, usually of a young woman.
parole.testo: Since early 1800s commonly used by Pennsylvania Dutch (Penslfawnisch Deitsch); possibly a borrowing from dialectal German dutzig, also dützig, ditzig (“numb, dazed, dizzy, as after having been punched; dull, stupid”), from dialectal dutzen (“to butt, hit, punch”). parole.significato: A ship prefix used for Nazi Germany's Kriegsmarine.
parole.testo: From German DKM, from German Deutsche Kriegsmarine, from deutsch+Kriegsmarine, from Krieg+Marine.

parole.significato: A large breed of guard dog bred in Germany.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dobermann, from the name of Karl Friedrich Louis Dobermann, who first developed this breed. Dobermann was born "Tobermann." parole.significato: A documentary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dokumentation.

parole.significato: Aboard a ship, either of the two short two-hour watches that take place between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m.
parole.testo: From dog + watch, perhaps a calque of German Hundewache.

parole.significato: The bagpipes.
parole.testo: From German Dudelsack.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Dr. Heinz Doofenshmirtz, an affable, hapless mad scientist character from the 2007 American animate…
parole.testo: From Doofenshmirtz + -ian; the character's name is possibly inspired by doofus or German doof (“stupid”) and German surnames such as Schmitz.

parole.significato: A Bavarian speciality beer, deep gold to dark brown, with a large, creamy, persistent head and a strong malty aroma.
parole.testo: From German Doppelbock (“double bock”).

parole.significato: A ghostly double of a living person, especially one that haunts such a person.

parole.significato: A village in a German-speaking area.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the city of Dortmund, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.

parole.significato: A double standard.
parole.testo: Calque of German Doppelmoral or Spanish doble moral.

parole.significato: A doppelganger.

parole.significato: A gift given to placate someone, especially a spouse, who is angry at the giver.

parole.significato: The three-mora rule, specifying where to place the accent in Germanic words.

parole.significato: A strong, durable cotton fabric with a strong bias (diagonal) in the weave.

parole.significato: Major; in the major mode.

parole.significato: Synonym of duopoly.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the city of Düsseldorf, capital of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.

parole.significato: The branch of biology dealing with the relationships of organisms with their environment and with each other.

parole.significato: A first-person shooter.

parole.testo: From German eidetisch, from Ancient Greek εἰδητικός (eidētikós), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from German eigen (“own”). Many of the compounds represent partial translations from German, e.g. eigenvalue from German Eigenwert. Doublet of own.

parole.significato: A note having one-eighth the duration of a whole note; a quaver.

parole.significato: An extremely clever or intelligent person.

parole.testo: From German Einstein, the surname of Albert Einstein (1879–1955) + English -ian (suffix forming adjectives or nouns meaning ‘belonging to, relating to, or like’).

parole.significato: Development of a mechanized state of mind (for problem solving).

parole.testo: Calque of German Ellbogenmentalität or Ellenbogenmentalität, from Ellbogen / Ellenbogen (“elbow”) + Mentalität (“mentality”).

parole.significato: A process by which two cultural forms (e.g. religious, intellectual, political or economic) having certain similarities…
parole.testo: Calque of German Wahlverwandtschaft.

parole.significato: A situation in which one truck tries to overtake another at a slightly higher speed, blocking the road for passenger ca…

parole.significato: Synonym of hendecad.
parole.testo: Equivalent to German elf (“eleven”) + Beine (“legs”).

parole.significato: Any member of the species Triticum dicoccum, one of a group of hulled wheats that are important food grains.

parole.significato: Synonym of Empfindsamkeit.

parole.significato: The German energy transition, a change in national energy policy in favor of renewable sources and energy efficiency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Energiewende (“energy transition”).

parole.significato: A postulated physical or biochemical change in neural tissue that represents a memory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Engramm which was coined by German evolutionary biologist Richard Semon in 1904. First attested in English in 1921 (see quotation below). Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + γράμμα (grámma, “writing, picture”).

parole.significato: Torture performed at detainees by the US Armed Forces.
parole.testo: Coined the George W. Bush administration, with the antecedent German verschärfte Vernehmung (“enhanced interrogation”). Compare enhanced interrogation.

parole.significato: A dog of a breed traditionally used by herders in the Swiss Alps.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Entlebucher Sennenhund, from Entlebuch, a municipality in the canton of Lucerne in Switzerland.

parole.significato: A measure of the disorder present in a system.
parole.testo: First attested in 1867, as the translation of German Entropie, coined in 1865 by Rudolph Clausius in analogy to Energie (“energy”), replacing the root of Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon, “work”) by Ancient Greek τροπή (tropḗ, “transformation”)).

parole.significato: A decision problem of finding a way to decide whether a formula is true or provable within a given system.

parole.significato: A red, acidic dye commonly used in histological stains.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Eosin, coined by Heinrich Caro, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in.

parole.significato: A white blood cell responsible for combating parasitic infections in the body.
parole.testo: From German eosinophil, from eosin (“rose dye, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in”) + -o- + -phil.

parole.significato: A critique of a critique; a metacritique.

parole.testo: Partial calque of German Erlkönig (literally “alder-king”), a mistranslation of Danish ellerkonge (“king of the elves”).

parole.significato: An ermine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Hermelin (“ermine”), from Middle High German hermelin, from Old High German harmilī, harmilīn (“weasel”), diminutive of Old High German harmo (“ermine, stoat, weasel”), from Proto-West Germanic *harmō, from Proto-Germanic *harmô (“weasel”). Cognate with Italian ermellino (“ermin

parole.significato: An inauthentic or inadequate substitute or imitation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ersatz (“replacement, substitute”), a back-formation from ersetzen (“to replace, to substitute”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ester, possibly a blend of Essig + Äther. See ether for more.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter ẞ/ß.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Eszett, from the names of the letters S and Z which make up its blackletter form.
