parole.testo: Borrowed from German Ethnosexismus, introduced by Gabriele Dietze 2016 in reference to the discourses around 2015–16 New Year's Eve sexual assaults in Germany. Equivalent to ethno- + sexism.

parole.significato: The univalent hydrocarbon radical, C₂H₅, formally derived from ethane by the loss of a hydrogen atom.
parole.testo: From German Ethyl, from Ether + -yl.

parole.significato: A yellow pigment in plants grown without sufficient light; a precursor of chlorophyll.
parole.testo: From German Etiolin; etiolate + -in.

parole.significato: A derivative of cocaine used as a local anesthetic in veterinary medicine.
parole.testo: From German Eukain; comparable to eu- + -caine.

parole.significato: A trump card game played by four players in two partnerships with a reduced deck of 24 cards.
parole.testo: Possibly from German Juckerspiel, name of an eighteenth-century Alsatian card game, itself apparently a compound of Jucker + Spiel (“game”). Likely a doublet of joker.

parole.significato: A breed of dog of the spitz type that originated in Germany.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Eurasier (“Eurasian”), signifying the breed’s European and Asian background.

parole.significato: A worldwide change in sea level, especially one caused by melting ice or tectonic activity.
parole.testo: A back-formation from eustatic (borrowed from German eustatische (“eustatic”), from Ancient Greek εὖ (eû, “well, good”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”)) + -y.

parole.significato: The outer layer of a pollen grain or spore; the exosporium.
parole.testo: From German Exine, from Latin ex- + German -ine.

parole.significato: Existence; state of existing.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from German Existenz. Doublet of existence.

parole.significato: To deregister or unenroll (a student in Germany or Austria), as a result of graduation, expulsion, or voluntary termina…
parole.testo: From German exmatrikulieren, equivalent to ex- + matriculate.

parole.significato: A variation of speedcore with a bpm exceeding 1000.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German extrahieren (“to extract”) + Tone (“notes”).

parole.significato: An extroverted person: one who is outgoing, sociable, and concerned with outer affairs.
parole.testo: Alteration of earlier extravert (by influence of introvert), from German Extravert, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's 1918 "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte". By surface analysis, extro- + -vert.

parole.significato: The graphical features of musical scores that when performed are unnoticeable by the listener.
parole.testo: Calque of German Augenmusik.

parole.significato: A (narrow) specialist expert who is ignorant outside of their specialty, or who only looks at problems through the (bli…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fachidiot.

parole.significato: a kind of polonaise, associated with German royal wedding celebrations
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fackeltanz (“torch dance”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being a fact.
parole.testo: From fact + -icity, possibly modelled on German Faktizität which first appeared in the writings of the German philosopher Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814).

parole.significato: A stratum in crystalline rock that contains metallic sulfides.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fahlband.

parole.significato: fahlband
parole.testo: From German Fahlerz.

parole.significato: Describing a temperature scale originally defined as having 0°F as the lowest temperature obtainable with a mixture of…
parole.testo: From German Fahrenheit, named after Prussian scientist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit.

parole.significato: Driving pleasure, especially with regard to Volkswagen vehicles.
parole.testo: An unadapted borrowing from German Fahrvergnügen, from fahren (“to drive”) + Vergnügen (“pleasure”); popularized in the US by Volkswagen advertisements in the 1990s.

parole.significato: A faulty understanding of the true character of social processes due to ideology.
parole.testo: Calque of German falsches Bewusstsein, as used by Friedrich Engels in a letter to Franz Mehring (1893).

parole.significato: A kind of collapsible canoe.
parole.testo: From German Faltboot, literally "folding boat".

parole.significato: A romantic story about a given family.
parole.testo: From family + romance, in psychoanalytic sense after German Familienroman.

parole.significato: A serving of this drink.
parole.testo: Marketing coinage, derived from German Fantasie (“imagination”), which employees were exhorted to use in inventing a name for the new drink.

parole.significato: A German sponge cake with Fanta as the key ingredient.
parole.testo: Calque of German Fantakuchen.

parole.significato: One who farsees; prophet; soothsayer; fortuneteller.
parole.testo: Modelled after German Fernseher (“TV set”, literally “farseer”), from Fernsehen (“television”, literally “farsee”), calque of French télévision, from Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “far away”) and Latin visio (“sight”). By surface analysis, far + seer.

parole.significato: Wanderlust; yearning for far-off places.
parole.testo: Calque of German Fernweh; contrast homesickness.

parole.significato: Partially fermented grape must.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Federweißer.

parole.significato: The greenish-grey colour of German military uniforms.
parole.testo: From German Feldgrau, literally "field-grey".

parole.significato: Any of a large group of rock-forming aluminosilicate minerals containing potassium, sodium, or calcium that, together,…
parole.testo: Partial calque of German Feldspat, formed from Feld (“field”) + Spat (“spar”), the second element replaced with the English cognate spar.

parole.significato: Containing feldspar.
parole.testo: From German Feldspath (“feldspar”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Any of a small group of igneous, plutonic, and volcanic minerals formed in magma that did not contain enough silica to…
parole.testo: From German Feldspath (“feldspar”) + -oid.

parole.significato: A German sergeant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Feldwebel.

parole.significato: A blockfield.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Felsenmeer, literally "sea of rock".

parole.significato: Felsite.
parole.testo: From German Feldstein, in analogy with English feldspar.

parole.significato: A guitar produced by the Fender company, a manufacturer of electric guitars.
parole.testo: From German, a variant of Fenrich or Fendler.

parole.significato: A geologic structure formed by erosion or normal faulting on a thrust system; a tectonic window.
parole.testo: From German Fenster (“window”), from Latin fenestra (“window”).

parole.significato: A gathering for a specified reason or occasion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fest (“feast, festival, party”), from Middle High German fëst, from Latin festum, from which last are also English feast, festival, festivity, fete, fiesta (see these).

parole.significato: A kind of beer, a helles lager.
parole.testo: From German Festbier.

parole.significato: A collection of articles, essays, etc., published together as a memorial or tribute to an academic or some other respec…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Festschrift, from Fest (“celebration; festival”) + Schrift (“writing (work of an author)”).

parole.significato: In certain nations the highest military rank, ranking below only the commander-in-chief; now mostly disused, being rese…
parole.testo: From field + marshal, calque of German Feldmarschall or its source, Middle French maréchal de camp.

parole.significato: A small shrill pipe, resembling the piccolo flute, used chiefly to accompany the drum in military music
parole.testo: From German Pfeife (“whistle, smoking pipe”). Doublet of pipe.

parole.significato: To complete a form or questionnaire with requested information.
parole.testo: In the sense of to complete a form, originally attested in American English; possibly as a calque of German ausfüllen. Later spread to British English, where it now competes with the traditional expression fill in.

parole.significato: The planned and attempted mass murder of the European Jews by the Nazis; the Holocaust.
parole.testo: Calque of German Endlösung, which is short for Endlösung der Judenfrage (“Final Solution to the Jewish Question”)

parole.significato: A contemptible person.
parole.testo: Unknown; first attested in 1894. A connection to Yiddish as some propose is unlikely. Suggested origins include: * German Fink (“finch; frivolous or dissolute person; informer”) as finches are notoriously chatty birds in groups. If so, then Doublet of finch. Compare canary (“informer”). * Partly fro

parole.significato: The process by which a smaller or less powerful sovereign state comes to abide by a more powerful neighbor's foreign po…
parole.testo: From Finland + -ization, translating German Finnlandisierung, referring to the political climate in Finland during the cold war in the view of a 1960s and 1970s West-German debate.

parole.testo: From fire + wall. Compare West Frisian brânmuorre, Dutch brandmuur, German Brandmauer, Feuermauer, Swedish brandvägg, brandmur, Icelandic eldvegg. parole.testo: Borrowed from German Firn, from Alemannic German firn (“last year's”), from Old High German firni (“old”), from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *firnijaz, *fernaz (“foregoing, previous”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“forth, forward, across, through”); cognate with Old English fy

parole.significato: Ground-based anti-aircraft guns firing explosive shells.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German FlaK, short for Fliegerabwehrkanone (“anti airplane cannon”).

parole.significato: A device that projects a flame for starting fires, and sometimes also additional fuel to help ignition. Used either as…
parole.testo: From flame + thrower, calque of German Flammenwerfer.

parole.significato: tarte flambée, especially when served in a German setting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Flammkuchen.

parole.significato: To exhibit the flehmen response, i.e., to draw back the lips, allowing scent to reach the Jacobson’s organ, an auxiliar…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German flehmen.

parole.significato: Flaring of the lip in mammals, associated with intensive smelling; flehming.
parole.testo: From German flehmen, from Upper Saxon German flemmen (“to look spiteful”).

parole.significato: A brass instrument resembling a cornet but with a wider, conical bore, and usually with three valves, in the same B-fla…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Flügelhorn, from Flügel (“wing, flank”) + horn.

parole.significato: A device used to measure the fluorescence of a solution.
parole.testo: From fluoro- + -scope, originally after German Fluorescop.

parole.significato: A series of sandstones and schists overlying the true nummulitic formation in the Alps, and included in the Eocene Tert…
parole.testo: From German fließen (“to flow, to melt”).

parole.significato: To cheat, to deceive, to trick, to take in, to impose upon someone.
parole.testo: From German foppen (“to mock”).

parole.significato: A warm dry wind blowing down the north sides of the Alps, especially in Switzerland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Föhn, from Old High German phonno, from Vulgar Latin faōnius, an alteration of Latin favōnius (“west wind”), from Favōnius (“Roman wind god”).

parole.significato: The uncertainty in situational awareness experienced by participants in military operations.
parole.testo: Calque of German Nebel des Krieges, an expression coined by Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz.

parole.significato: A popular explanation for the origin of a term which has been rejected as false by expert etymologists.
parole.testo: English from the 1880s (Abram Smythe Palmer, 1882), a calque of German Volksetymologie (1820s, in 1821 as Volks-Etymologie in J. A. Schmeller's Die Mundarten Bayerns grammatisch dargestellt).

parole.significato: character of a people, folklore, that which defines a people’s original nature and culture (or an individual's tie to i…
parole.testo: From folk + -dom, a calque of German Volkstum. In German, only sense 2 is associated with Nazism.

parole.significato: Invention or adaptation of folklore, including any use of a tradition outside the cultural context in which it was crea…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Folklorismus.

parole.significato: Synonym of folklorism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Folklorismus.

parole.significato: table soccer (US), table football (UK)
parole.testo: From German Fußball, itself a calque of English football.

parole.significato: Infantry.
parole.testo: Calque of German Fußvolk.

parole.significato: Next to last, second to last.
parole.testo: From fore- + last. In some instances of more recent use, perhaps also a calque of German vorletzte or Dutch voorlaatst.

parole.significato: A pear cultivar
parole.testo: From German Forelle (“trout”), because of its speckled coloration.

parole.significato: troctolite

parole.significato: Synonym of formative (“language unit, typically a morph, that has a morphological function”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Formans, from Latin elementum fōrmāns (“forming element”), with fōrmāns being the present participle of fōrmō (“to shape; to form; to fashion”). Doublet of formant.

parole.significato: A band of frequencies in a sound spectrum that have greater intensity and determine the quality of a sound, especially…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Formant, from Latin fōrmāns (“shaping; forming; fashioning”), present participle of fōrmō (“to shape; to form; to fashion”). Doublet of formans.

parole.significato: A thing which causes formation to occur.
parole.testo: Etymology 2 sense 1 (“thing which causes formation to occur”) is derived from the noun. Etymology 2 sense 2.1 (“language unit”) is borrowed from German Formativ, a noun use of formativ (adjective), from Middle French formatif, from Old French formatif (see etymology 1).

parole.significato: Any of a certain kind of scholarship or fellowship granted by some German academic Stiftungen to fund or subsidize a sp…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Forschungsstipendium.

parole.significato: The (repeated) disappearance and reappearance of an object, especially as a source of pleasure in child play.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German fort (“gone”) and da (“there”), exclamations that Sigmund Freud heard his grandson utter while playing, described in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920).

parole.significato: The cryptanalysis of an Enigma message which was a continuation of a previous message sent at a known time.
parole.testo: From a message whose plaintext began fortyweepyyweepy: German fort (“forth”), short for Fortsetzung (“continuation”) + weep, typewriter code for 23:30, the time of the previous message. Enigma machines had no number keys, so the letter y marked the letters to be interpreted as numbers.

parole.significato: A style of black letter type, used especially in German-speaking countries from the 16th century until World War II.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1886 as fractur, and c. 1904 as fraktur, from German Fraktur, from Latin frāctūra (“breaking”, noun), from frangere (“to break”), past participle fractus. Compare English fracture, fraction. Doublet of fracture.

parole.significato: A monster composed of body parts from various corpses attached and brought back to life by a mad scientist, typically s…
parole.testo: From German Frankenstein, various places named for Franken (“Franks, Frankish”) + Stein (“stone”). parole.significato: A frankfurter; a hot dog sausage.
parole.testo: From German Frankfurt. Compare frankfurter.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the city of Frankfurt, state of Hesse, Germany.
parole.testo: From German Frankfurter. Equivalent to Frankfurt + -er.

parole.significato: A moist sausage of soft, even texture and flavor, often made from mechanically recovered meat or meat slurry.
parole.testo: From German Frankfurter, the demonym of Frankfurt. Specifically, a reference to Frankfurt-am-Main.

parole.significato: A kind of German cinnamon roll pastry, similar to a croissant, originating from Hamburg.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Franzbrötchen.

parole.significato: The droppings or excrement of insect larvae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fraß.

parole.significato: Used as a courtesy title before the surname of a (typically married) German-speaking woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Frau.

parole.significato: A woman, especially a German woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Frau. Doublet of frow, vrou, and vrouw.

parole.significato: A young German woman.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fräulein.

parole.significato: Synonym of Freikorps.
parole.testo: Calque of German Freikorps.

parole.significato: A self-ruling city within the Holy Roman Empire that had some autonomy and was represented in the Imperial Diet.
parole.testo: A calque of German Freie Reichsstadt (short singular form of Freie und Reichsstädte) or Latin urbs imperialis libera.

parole.significato: A political entity whose political status is less than that of a fully sovereign nation-state, as with the former Congo…
parole.testo: From free + state, probably a calque of German Freistaat.

parole.significato: A provision in copyright law that permits taking photographs or video footage, or creating other images (such as painti…
parole.testo: Calque of German Panoramafreiheit.

parole.significato: A German-speaking corps of military or paramilitary and free (autonomous) nature, in some cases a private militia or ar…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from German Freikorps.

parole.significato: A feeling of vicarious embarrassment for another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fremdschämen (verb) or Fremdschämen (noun).

parole.significato: Rude, cheeky, or inappropriate; presumptuous; disrespectful; forward.

parole.significato: to eat without restraint; eat heartily
parole.testo: From German fressen (“to eat, devour, gobble”) and/or Yiddish פֿרעסן (fresn), both from Middle High German vrëȥȥen, from Old High German frëȥȥan (“to eat up”), from Proto-West Germanic *fraetan, from Proto-Germanic *fraetaną (“to eat up”), from *fra- (intensive and perfective prefix) + *etaną (“to e

parole.significato: A German person, usually male.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fritz, pet form of Friedrich (“Frederick”).

parole.significato: An Internet aesthetic characterized by modern and organic themes associated with nature, glass, water and air.
parole.testo: Coined by Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute member Sofi Lee in 2017. From Frutiger (“a sans-serif typeface”), from German Frutiger, the surname of its designer in turn meaning “of Frutigen”, and (Windows) Aero (“a design language”), a backronym for Authentic, Energetic, Reflective, and Open.

parole.significato: The member of a military group who leads the way or demonstrates drill; hence, someone who keeps the beat or timing, an…
parole.testo: From earlier flugleman, flugelman, from German Flügelmann (“a file-leader”), from Flügel (“a wing, file”) + Mann (“man”).

parole.significato: An ablaut form that is either e-grade or o-grade.
parole.testo: From full + grade, as in gradation (“apophony”). Possibly after German Vollstufe.

parole.significato: Synonym of human right, sometimes with subtle differences.
parole.testo: While the term itself occurs often enough in the 17th century already, it isn’t always with the same meaning and it is problematic to trace how it became a set term. parole.significato: The practice of sending deceptive information to the enemy by means of their official channels that have been subverted.
parole.testo: From German Funkspiel; originally the name of a Nazi counterintelligence operation during World War II.

parole.significato: A sense of joy or wellbeing an animal (including a human) gets from doing that which it is meant to do.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Funktionslust.

parole.significato: A mixture of several higher-order alcohols (having more than two carbon atoms) formed as byproduct in the normal fermen…
parole.testo: Partial calque of German Fuselöl, from Fusel, referring to low-quality alcoholic beverages in general, especially to inferior wines and spirits distilled with inadequate equipment.

parole.significato: Synonym of fusel oil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fuselöl.

parole.significato: The scientific forecasting of future trends in science, technology or society
parole.testo: From future + -ology. Attested once in 1934 as the title of play, Futureology; in later use, after German Futurologie, suggested in a 1942 letter to the American scholar John H. Herz by the German political scientist Ossip K. Flechtheim, who used futurology in a 1943 Phylon article.

parole.significato: Adolf Hitler, during his time as chancellor of Nazi Germany.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from German Führer, modelled after Italian Duce. Doublet of farer.

parole.significato: Synonym of pentad.
parole.testo: Equivalent to German fünf (“five”) + Beine (“legs”). Compare German fünfbeinig (“five-legged”).

parole.significato: The base form of a verb (as opposed to its extended verb forms), particularly in the Semitic languages
parole.testo: From German Grundstamm.

parole.significato: the base form of a verb (as opposed to its extended verb forms), particularly in Semitic languages
parole.testo: From German Grundstamm (“basic stem”).

parole.significato: The offset and typically most distal tooth on the fixed digits of mesostigmatan mites.
parole.testo: From German Gabel (“fork”) + a misspelling of Zahn (“tooth”).

parole.significato: To add sugar and water to (unfermented grape juice) so as to increase the quantity of wine produced.
parole.testo: From German Gall + English -ize (suffix forming verbs from adjectives or nouns with the sense of doing what the adjective or noun denotes), from the surname of Dr. Ludwig Gall (1791–1863), the German inventor who developed the process.

parole.significato: A tuft of chamois or other hair traditionally worn as a decoration on hats in alpine Austria and Bavaria.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Gamsbart.

parole.significato: A particular phenomenon of visual perception, the ganzfeld effect.
parole.testo: From German, meaning "complete field", from ganz + Feld.

parole.significato: A recorder whose lowest note is C₆ (or otherwise in the range of B♭₅ to D₆).
parole.testo: From German garklein (“very small”), from (archaic) gar (“very”) + klein (“small”).

parole.significato: A German inn or guesthouse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Gasthaus.

parole.significato: Synonym of food critic.
parole.testo: From gastro- + critic, a calque of German Gastrokritiker and Russian гастрокритик (gastrokritik).

parole.significato: A stage in the development of embryos of most animals consisting of a three-layered sac of ectoderm, mesoderm and endod…
parole.testo: From German Gastrula, coined by Ernst Haeckel in his 1872 work "Biology of Calcareous Sponges". From gastr- (from Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”) + Latin -ula.

parole.significato: The stage of embryo development at which a gastrula is formed from the blastula by the inward migration of cells.
parole.testo: From German Gastrulation, coined by Ernst Haeckel in his 1872 work "Biology of Calcareous Sponges" (see also gastrula).

parole.significato: District, region.
parole.testo: From German Gau, from Middle High German göu, gou, from Old High German gawi.

parole.significato: An official in charge of a district of the Nazi Party (after 1933 increasingly adopting state functions).
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Gauleiter, from Gau (“administrative division”) + Leiter (“leader”).

parole.significato: Music composed for a specific, identifiable purpose, not just for its own sake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Gebrauchsmusik (literally “utility music”).

parole.significato: thought experiment
parole.testo: From German Gedankenexperiment (“thought experiment”), from Gedanke (“thought”) + Experiment (“experiment”).

parole.significato: paratonia
parole.testo: From German Gegenhalten.

parole.significato: A counterion: an ion of opposite charge to another in an electrochemical or ion transport system.
parole.testo: From the German gegen (“against”) + ion.

parole.significato: A tactic in which a team, after losing possession of the ball, immediately attempts to win back possession, rather than…

parole.significato: A faint brightening of the night sky in the region of the ecliptic directly opposite the Sun.

parole.significato: Theory of objects.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Gegenstandstheorie.

parole.significato: Humic acid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Geïn, coined by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1832, from Ancient Greek γήινος (gḗinos, “of earth”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”).

parole.significato: A ghost, an apparition.
parole.testo: From German Geist (“spirit, ghost, mind”). Doublet of ghost.

parole.significato: terrain, area.

parole.testo: Calque of German Hochalemannisch. By surface analysis, high + Alemannic.

parole.significato: A wine from Hochheim am Main, Germany.

parole.significato: A Grand Master of the Teutonic Order.
parole.testo: From German Hochmeister.

parole.significato: High-born; aristocratic, of noble birth.

parole.significato: A Rhenish white wine.

parole.significato: Primitive forms of agriculture defined by the absence of the plough.

parole.significato: An enclosure, court, dwelling, building, or house.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Hof. Doublet of howff.

parole.significato: A member of the Hohenzollern family and dynasty.
parole.testo: From German Hohenzollern.

parole.significato: A cavity whose walls are in thermodynamic equilibrium with the radiation emitted by the cavity

parole.significato: An ecosystem in Friederichs' theory of nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Holocoen. Equivalent to holo- (“all”) + Ancient Greek κοινός (koinós, “together”). Confer abiocoen.

parole.significato: An organism which is purely a saprophyte.
parole.testo: From German Holosaprophyt, equivalent to holo- (“whole”) + sapro- (“putric, rotten”) + -phyte (“plant”).

parole.significato: A system of treating diseases with small amounts of substances which, in larger amounts, would produce the observed sym…
parole.testo: From German Homöopathie, equivalent to English homeo- + -pathy.

parole.testo: Calque of German Heimweh (“homesickness”, literally “home-woe”), equivalent to home + sickness.

parole.significato: An entirely human world-view, with no elements that do not reflect human senses and experience, especially with the bel…
parole.testo: From Latin homo (“man”) + -ism, to avoid confusion with humanism, already taken in established meanings. Some senses were first invented in German Hominismus.

parole.testo: From homosexual + -ity, equivalent to homo- + sexuality and after the model of German Homosexualität, coined by journalist Karl Maria Kertbeny in 1869, and French homosexualité, attested in 1891.

parole.significato: A vacuum cleaner, irrespective of brand.

parole.significato: The now-discredited principle that the body will not harm itself by its own immune reactions.
parole.testo: Latinate neologism coined c. 1900 by Paul Ehrlich in German, from Latin horror, auto- (“self”), toxicus (“toxic”). Compare horror vacui.

parole.significato: A block of the Earth's crust, bounded by faults, that has been raised relative to the surrounding area.
parole.testo: From German Horst (“heap”). Doublet of hurst.

parole.significato: A housewife.

parole.significato: The study of the humanities or the liberal arts; literary (especially classical) scholarship.

parole.significato: A composition that is playful in attitude and tone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Humoreske.

parole.significato: Any hypergolic propellant.

parole.significato: A mild form of mania, especially the phase of several mood disorders characterized by euphoria or hyperactivity.

parole.significato: The state of one's own self or identity; one's conscious personality.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the central government of Austria-Hungary.

parole.testo: From German Inkludenz, a 1960s neologism coined by Hubertus Tellenbach, derived from Latin inclūdō (“confine, imprison”).

parole.significato: Self-referentiality.

parole.testo: After a German term coined by Ferdinand Christian Baur in an 1831 issue of the Tübinger Zeitschrift für Theologie.

parole.significato: A coffee klatch.

parole.testo: Borrowed from German Karrenfeld, from Karre + -n- + Feld.

parole.significato: Synonym of cat organ.

parole.significato: A mass or shred of chromatin-staining material outside of the nucleus in the cytoplasm.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a marine environment of shallow waters.

parole.significato: Synonym of ennead.

parole.testo: From German Neutrophil, from neutro- (“neutro-”) + -phil (“-phile”), equivalent to neutro- + -phil.

parole.significato: Do not change something while it is working (because there is a risk of breaking it).

parole.significato: A silvery elemental metal with an atomic number of 28 and symbol Ni.

parole.significato: A purge, in which opponents of a regime or political party are killed or removed.

parole.significato: Government that is limited to a bare minimum of functions, usually just military, police, and courts.
parole.testo: Calque of German Nachtwächterstaat, which was coined by German socialist Ferdinand Lassalle in an 1862 speech in Berlin. He used this term to criticize the idea of a state with minimal government, comparing it to a night watchman whose sole duty was preventing theft.

parole.testo: Borrowed from German Nihilartikel, apparently coined as a hoax in the German-language Wikipedia in 2003 and later picked up by the English Wikipedia, from where it spread to blogs, books, etc., which are now used again as references for these sites, leading to a form of citogenesis.

parole.significato: A form of stainless steel typically used to make blades.

parole.significato: A scatterbrained or stupid person.

parole.significato: Nothing.

parole.significato: Zoropsis spinimana, a relatively large hunting spider originally from southern Europe.

parole.significato: An enlarged part of the avian brain that is involved in vision; the hyperpallium.

parole.significato: A cabinet of scientific curiosities, especially during the late Renaissance.
parole.testo: From German Wunderkammer (literally “room of wonders”).

parole.significato: A child prodigy; a wonderchild.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from German Wunderkind, from Wunder (“wonder”) + Kind (“child”). Compare native wonderchild.

Akin to Old Saxon worst (“wurst”), Old English weor

parole.significato: A rural, unsophisticated person; a bumpkin.
parole.testo: From German Wurzel (“root”), via mangelwurzel, a root crop cultivated for livestock feed beginning in the 18th century.

parole.significato: A vascular tissue in land plants primarily responsible for the distribution of water and minerals taken up by the roots…
parole.testo: From German Xylem, from Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”).

parole.significato: Yeah; yes.
parole.testo: Apparently from German ja and cognates in other Germanic languages; related to English yeah.

parole.significato: A heavy, muzzle-loading hunting rifle

parole.significato: Century (a hundred-year timespan).

parole.significato: A person from or living in the countryside, viewed as being unsophisticated or naive.

parole.significato: To be frivolous and waste time.
parole.testo: From German herumfurzen (literally “to fart around”) (herum- + furzen), perhaps via Yiddish אַרומפֿאַרצן (arumfartsn); alternatively, a euphemism for fuck.

parole.significato: A (type of) linen cloth historically exported from Germany.
parole.testo: A corruption of a placename, probably German Görlitz in Silesia (whence early spellings like garlits), or possibly Dutch Gulik (the Duchy of Jülich, suggested by early spellings like gulix).

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining, to a Green Party or green party.
parole.testo: English surname, a topographic name for someone who either lived near a village green, or was just fond of the colour. parole.significato: Anti-Semitism, a hatred of Jews.
parole.testo: Calque of German Judenhass or from Jew + hatred; the alternative form of Jewhatred in particular was influenced by German Judenhass (“Jew-hatred”).

parole.significato: A military barracks, especially of the US military, in Germany.
parole.testo: From German Kaserne, or alteration of casern under the influence of that German word. In either case, ultimately from French caserne. Doublet of casern.

parole.significato: An iron bucket used in mines for hoisting anything to the surface.
parole.testo: From German Kübel (“pail”), from Middle High German kübel, kubel (“bucket, bushel, measure of grain”), from Old High German kubil (“tub, bucket”), from Proto-West Germanic *kubil, from Proto-Germanic *kub- (“to be vaulted, arch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew-, *gū- (“to bend, curve, arch, vault”).

parole.significato: An improvised device, typically crudely constructed to test the validity of a principle before implementing a finished…
parole.testo: Perhaps from British military slang, possibly based on Scots word kludge or kludgie (“common toilet”), or perhaps from German klug (“clever”). parole.significato: A pair of knee-breeches made of leather, typical of Bavaria and Austria.
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Lederhose (literally “leather trousers”). The final -n probably from the German plural; alternatively influenced by Bavarian Lederhosn (singular and plural).

parole.significato: A hump or bump on a skiing piste.
parole.testo: From dialectal German Mugel or from dialectal Norwegian mugje (“heap, mound”).

parole.significato: A crystalline alkaloid (4,5-epoxy-17-methyl-7,8-didehydromorphinan-3,6-diol), extracted from opium, the salts of which…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French morphine or German Morphin, from Ancient Greek Μορφεύς (Morpheús, “the god and personification of dreams”).

parole.significato: Paragnathi (lobes forming the lower lip, or metastome, of Crustacea).
parole.testo: Apparently from para- + -gnath + -a, after either German Paragnathen pl or French paragnathes pl. Compare later paragnath and paragnathus.

parole.significato: Any of various card games in which, following each of one or more rounds of dealing or revealing cards, the players in…
parole.testo: American English, perhaps from first element of German Pochspiel, from German pochen, perhaps from French poque. First appeared in the 19th century.

parole.significato: A member of any of several Christian denominations which separated from the Roman Catholic Church based on theological…
parole.testo: Borrowed from either German Protestant or French protestant, one likely reinforced by the other; equivalent to protest + -ant.

parole.significato: A penis, especially a long one.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Yiddish שלאַנג (shlang, “snake”; by extension, “a penis”) or German Schlange.

parole.significato: To leave in a hurry; to go away.
parole.testo: Probably either: * a clipping of scramble by apocope; or * from dialectal German schramm, the imperative singular form of schrammen (“to scratch, scrape”), from Late Middle High German schramm, schramme (“a graze, scratch”); further etymology unknown.

parole.significato: A small-scale symphony (either in length or size of orchestra needed).
parole.testo: Either: * from Italian sinfonietta; * formed on the Italian roots sinfonia (“symphony”) + -etta (feminine diminutive suffix), either in English or in German (as Sinfonietta) and adopted thence; or, * an alteration of the French symphoniette to resemble an Italian construction of the form sinfonia +

parole.significato: Barrier.
parole.testo: Probably a calque of Dutch slagboom or German Schlagbaum. These are etymologically equivalent to English slay + beam, meaning a beam that can be banged (“slain”) down. parole.testo: Spotted refers to the dried fruits (that resemble spots). Dick is a dialectal term for "pudding". parole.testo: Uncertain. parole.significato: millennium (a thousand-year timespan)
parole.testo: From year + thousand, a calque of either Latin millennium (from mīllennis, “thousand-year”), or, more probably, of a Germanic-language term (most likely from German); compare Dutch jaarduizend, German Jahrtausend, Norwegian årtusen, Icelandic árþúsund, and Swedish årtusende, all meaning “millennium”
